title: Sixth commandment (CCC 2337–2347)
hookLine: chastity as integration, the person whole and at peace

cards: A guitar sits on a stand by the window. Five strings are in tune; one has slipped, just slightly. Play any chord, and the whole thing sounds a little wrong, though it's hard to say why.
Tighten that one string, and every chord rings. Nothing was added. Something was brought into agreement with the rest.
Today's word can sound like only a no. The Catechism describes it as a kind of tuning.

teach.b: The commandment in the Douay-Rheims is brief: "Thou shalt not commit adultery." The Catechism reads it widely, and opens with a word that might surprise: chastity.

It defines chastity as the successful integration of sexuality within the person, and so the inner unity of a human being in body and spirit. The person, whole. Sexuality, in this teaching, isn't the enemy.
It becomes personal and truly human when it's woven into the relationship of one person to another, in the complete and lifelong gift of a man and a woman to each other.
Chastity tolerates neither a double life nor duplicity in speech: someone who lives one way in public and another in private isn't whole.
The Catechism calls chastity an apprenticeship in self-mastery, a training in human freedom. Either we govern our passions and find peace, or we let them rule us.
And it's honest that this is long work: self-mastery is never acquired once and for all. It takes effort at every stage of life, with its own stages and setbacks.
It's a virtue, and also a gift, a grace from the Holy Spirit. The last note is the warmest.
Chastity blossoms in friendship: a person at peace inside can be a true friend, giving without grabbing.

Elsewhere the Catechism adds that every baptized person is called to chastity, each according to their state of life: married, single or consecrated. Like the string on the guitar: not removed, brought into tune.

how: Catholics are taught that chastity is for everyone, lived differently by the married, the single and the consecrated; it's supported by prayer, confession, friendship and modesty.

games.q: you've kept up a public face that doesn't match your private life. nothing's been found out. what does the Catechism say chastity asks?
o: keep the two lives separate; no harm done.
no double life: let words and life become one.
confess publicly to everyone at once.
games.why: the Catechism says chastity tolerates neither a double life nor duplicity in speech: the point is a whole person.

practice: Think of the people you'll see today, at work, on the street, on a screen, and notice how easily a person can shrink to one thing: a body, a job title, an obstacle.

Choose one and let them grow back to full size in your mind, someone's child, with a history, hopes, a tired day. If you pray, ask for the grace to see people whole; if not, simply hold that one person, whole, for a moment.

wordCard.voice: Chastity. The integration of sexuality within the person: body and spirit at one, no double life, a self-mastery that frees a person for friendship and gift. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: purity, chastity; the Church's word for this virtue.

carryVoice: Your line: whole, not divided. Self-mastery takes a lifetime, and grace helps all along the way. Until tomorrow.
